title: Ultrasonic Testing for Petrochemical Plants | UT (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for US chemical and petrochemical plants: carbon steel, stainless and alloys. Request a UT quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Petrochemical and Chemical Plants in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to US chemical and petrochemical plants to measure wall thickness on process piping, reactors, columns and storage vessels, and to examine welds in repairs and tie-ins. The work covers carbon steel, stainless and mixed-metallurgy systems in olefins, polymers, aromatics and specialty chemical units, and supports the mechanical integrity records plants keep under OSHA PSM and EPA RMP. Request a UT inspection quote with your circuit list.

How a chemical plant differs from a refinery

A refinery processes one feedstock into many products with a fairly familiar set of damage mechanisms. A chemical complex runs dozens of unrelated chemistries side by side, each with its own corrosion behavior, and the piping stock reflects that: carbon steel next to 304 and 316 stainless, duplex, nickel alloys and lined or clad equipment, all inside one fence. Thickness testing in this setting is less about a standard list of units and more about getting the right couplant, calibration block and probe for each material, then keeping the readings traceable. For refinery-specific work, see UT for refineries.

Plant types and what we measure

  • Olefins plants. Quench water and compressor systems, caustic wash towers and cold-service piping. Furnace coils are a specialist scope that we do not perform; our work is the surrounding piping, vessels and columns.
  • Polymer plants. Polyethylene and polypropylene lines run at a range of pressures and see erosion at bends where pellets or slurry impact the wall, along with steam-traced piping that corrodes from outside.
  • Aromatics and derivatives. Benzene, toluene, xylene and their downstream products run in carbon steel with occasional stainless, and wall loss tends to follow velocity and water carryover.
  • Chlor-alkali, acids and ammonia. Aggressive services where the owner often specifies alloy piping and where wall thickness at bends and nozzles is a routine monitoring target.
  • Utilities. Cooling water, steam condensate and boiler feedwater piping that every plant has and every inspection program covers.
  • Tank farms and spheres. Shell thickness on atmospheric tanks and pressure spheres, with measurements at marked locations.

The mix of metals changes how we calibrate. Sound travels at different speeds in different alloys, so the velocity is set from a reference block of matching material, not copied from a carbon steel setting.

Regulations and codes behind the work

Most plants fall under OSHA process safety management in 29 CFR 1910.119, which requires inspection and testing of process equipment, documentation of the results, and correction of deficiencies. EPA's Risk Management Program rule at 40 CFR Part 68 applies a similar mechanical integrity obligation to covered processes. ASME Section VIII governs how vessels were designed and ASME B31.3 governs process piping; many plants adopt API 510 and API 570 as their in-service inspection standards even though the rules do not require them by name. Ultrasonic procedures follow ASME Section V Article 5 for thickness and Article 4 for weld examination. The API 510 support page and the API 570 support page describe the NDE data we supply; the authorized inspector or plant engineer owns the conclusions.

Technique details that matter in a chemical plant

  • Couplant control. Stainless and nickel alloys need couplant tested and certified low in halogens and sulfur, since residues can harm those metals in service. Water-based or specially certified gels are chosen per material and wiped off after the readings.
  • Calibration blocks. Each alloy gets its own step block. We note the block ID and material on the report.
  • Cladding and lining. On clad vessels, a reading through the cladding can mislead. The procedure states how the clad layer is handled, and we do not report base metal thickness unless the procedure supports it.
  • Surface condition. Painted piping with thin intact coating can be read with the right probe; flaking paint and scale cannot. Steam tracing and insulation jackets are removed by the owner's crew first.
  • Temperature. Hot lines get high-temperature couplant and a temperature note. Cold or sweating lines need dry, clean spots to couple the probe.
  • Grids and sweeps. Elbows, tees and reducers get a pattern of readings rather than a single point, because the thinnest spot rarely sits where the paint mark was drawn.
  • Weld examination. Angle-beam scanning is done to a written procedure; acceptance follows B31.3 or the vessel code, and the report states the criteria used.

Erosion, steam tracing and other plant-specific wall loss

Three kinds of wall loss show up in chemical plants more than refineries. Erosion at bends in polymer and slurry lines wears a smooth, localized groove at the outside of the elbow, so a ring of readings around the elbow matters more than a single point on the straight pipe. Steam-traced lines can corrode from the outside where the tracing contacts the pipe or where condensate pools under insulation. And heat-exchanger and cooling-water piping suffers from deposits that set up under-deposit corrosion, which gives rough, patchy backs that scatter sound. Each calls for a different pattern of readings, and we describe the pattern chosen in the report so the next campaign repeats it.

Plants with strict product purity, such as polymer and specialty chemical sites, add one more concern: nothing we apply may contaminate the product. Couplant is wiped off completely, probes are kept clean between materials, and we do not leave anything on open flanges or sampling points.

Weld examination on tie-ins and repairs

Chemical plants change constantly: a new pump, a rerouted line, an expansion tie-in. Each change brings new welds, and the owner's quality plan often asks for volumetric examination of a sample of them. Where radiography is not available to us, angle-beam ultrasonic scanning is the alternative for many butt welds in suitable thickness, as long as the code, the owner's specification and the material allow it. We agree on the acceptance criteria before the first scan, because a weld that is acceptable under one code may be rejectable under another, and a mid-job change of criteria wastes everyone's time. Thin-wall stainless and small-diameter piping may not be a good fit for angle-beam work, and we will say so rather than stretch the method.

Records and audits

When an OSHA or EPA auditor reviews a plant's mechanical integrity program, they ask for evidence that equipment was inspected as the plant said it would be, and for proof that deficiencies were corrected. Our reports are written to be read by an auditor who was not on site: they name the procedure, the instrument, the person and the criteria, and they show exactly where each reading was taken. We are happy to match your plant's CML numbering and data layout so reports load into your database without retyping.

If your question is about stainless surface cracking after a shutdown, the sibling pages above are the better fit. The complete ultrasonic testing guide explains the physics in more depth.

Planning inspections in an operating plant

Chemical plants run continuously for years between major outages, so a lot of thickness work is done on-stream, on the outside of lines in service. Our crew is mobilized for a defined scope, and the site's permit system decides when and where technicians can work. Expect safety orientation, TWIC at port-adjacent sites, personal gas monitors, and restrictions near lines carrying toxic or reactive fluids. Where a line is too hot, too cold, or too hazardous to approach, the circuit is deferred to the next outage. Scaffold, lifts and rope access are the site's to arrange. For outage-based scopes, see the turnaround and shutdown page.

What the report contains

  • Equipment tag or line number, matching the plant's isometric and CML numbering.
  • Material and nominal thickness, with the velocity or calibration block used for each alloy.
  • Procedure number, revision and governing code.
  • Instrument, probe and couplant lot, with calibration checks.
  • Readings by location, surface temperature, and prior readings where the plant supplies them.
  • Names of the Level II technician and the ASNT Level III reviewer.
  • Accept or reject for any weld indications, with a sketch of the position.

The report does not state remaining life. Atlantis does not calculate remaining life, set intervals or perform fitness-for-service assessments; those come from your engineer or authorized inspector using our data.

What to send us for a quote

  • Circuit list, isometrics or P&IDs with line numbers and equipment tags.
  • Materials by circuit, including alloys, lining and cladding.
  • Nominal thickness, operating temperature and the service fluid, if shareable.
  • Count of locations or circuits; weld examination scope if any.
  • Code or owner specification, and any limits on couplant or chemicals.
  • Access, insulation, tracing, scaffold and confined-space needs.
  • Site address, credentials and safety orientation, and the work window.

Where we work in the US for chemical plants

  • Houston: the center of the Gulf Coast petrochemical complex.
  • Beaumont: Southeast Texas chemical and polymer plants.
  • Baton Rouge: chemical plants along the Mississippi corridor.
  • Lake Charles: olefins and specialty chemical complexes.
  • Corpus Christi: coastal chemical and energy facilities.
  • New Orleans: river chemical plants and marine terminals nearby.
  • Louisville: a long-established chemical district on the Ohio River.
  • Chicago: Midwest chemical and polymer plants around the lakefront and Joliet area.

The shared tie-in is the circuit-by-circuit survey described on the ultrasonic pipe thickness testing page.

Training your own technicians

If your plant wants its own thickness testers, see UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 training, supported by the ultrasonic testing simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its people according to its own written practice, and we assist with written practice development. The manufacturing NDT training page outlines related programs.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not inspect furnace coils on this page, and does not offer specialist ultrasonic techniques here. We are not the authorized inspector of record. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: Can you do UT on stainless steel piping in a chemical plant?
faq.a: Yes. We calibrate on a block of the same alloy and use couplant certified low in halogens and sulfur, which protects stainless and nickel alloys, then clean the couplant off after the readings.

faq.q: What do you need to quote UT thickness testing on process piping?
faq.a: Send the circuit list or isometrics, materials, nominal wall, temperature, insulation or tracing status, access and your work window. The service fluid helps us plan safety and couplant.

faq.q: Do you work on running units?
faq.a: Often yes, on the outside of lines in service, if the site permits it and the surface temperature is within the probe and couplant limits. Hazardous or very hot lines are usually left for an outage.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 and EPA 40 CFR Part 68 drive the mechanical integrity program, while ASME Section V Article 5 and Article 4 govern thickness and weld UT. Plants often adopt API 510 and API 570 as well.

faq.q: Can UT measure thickness on clad or lined vessels?
faq.a: It can, but a reading through cladding or lining needs a procedure that says how to treat the layer. We do not report base metal thickness unless the procedure supports it.

faq.q: Who decides if a thickness is acceptable?
faq.a: The plant's authorized inspector or engineer decides, using minimum required thickness and corrosion rate. We provide readings and the report; we do not calculate remaining life.

faq.q: Do you inspect ethylene furnace tubes?
faq.a: No. Furnace coils are a specialist scope we do not offer. We cover the surrounding piping, columns and vessels with conventional contact ultrasonic testing, and the plant arranges the coil work separately with a specialist.

faq.q: Can the same crew also do MT or PT?
faq.a: Yes, and mixed-metallurgy plants usually need that. One mobilization can combine UT thickness, magnetic particle on carbon steel welds and penetrant on stainless welds, which saves repeated site credentials and travel.

faq.q: Do your technicians travel to plants outside the Gulf Coast?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your site anywhere in the United States, including Kentucky, the Great Lakes states and the Northeast, with lead time set by site credentials.
